title: 5 Key Takeaways from the F1 Invasion of the Nürburgring 24 Hours
meta: Published: 18 May 2026 | By Elena Vasquez, Chief Race Correspondent | F1CC News
caption: The Nordschleife hosted an unprecedented gathering of Formula 1 talent — here's what we learned.
body:
A Formula 1 championship leader funding his own Porsche. A four-time world champion returning from retirement. A dirt-track champion learning humility at 200 km/h in the dark. The 54th running of the ADAC Ravenol 24h Race at the Nürburgring was always going to be extraordinary, but nobody predicted quite how much the old circuit would teach the visitors from the pinnacle of motorsport. Here are the key takeaways from an eventful 24 hours in the Eifel.

01 — The Nordschleife Does Not Care About Your Day Job

For Eetu Väisänen, the 24h Nürburgring was much more than a side project. Leading the Formula 1 World Championship with Ferrari, the Finn had assembled a privateer Porsche 911 GT3 R with his own funding, recruited two fellow F1 drivers as co-drivers, and arrived in the Eifel with the quiet confidence of a man who had spent three months preparing for exactly this challenge.

The car was quick. The drivers were quick. But the Nordschleife, as it always does, found the gaps. Michiii MaraDöner, Greece's first F1 driver, took over at hour five and lasted until hour six and forty minutes before pushing two tenths beyond the limit at Adenauer Forst and finding the outside wall with the right rear quarter panel. The damage was repairable. The time cost was thirty-eight minutes. Väisänen's response on the radio was characteristically brief: "Good. Now drive the lap, not the corner."

MaraDöner drove the lap. By hour nine he had climbed to eleventh. The Porsche's tyre management — the car masking aggression in a way that no other platform in the field could quite match — began to show its advantage, and Väisänen himself took the final stint and delivered eighty-three minutes of lap times so consistent that the data engineers described them as unusual even by factory pro standards. The car finished ninth overall, fourth in Pro-Am.

"I learned that the Nordschleife doesn't care who you are," MaraDöner said afterward. "It doesn't care that you race in F1. It only cares if you respect it. I didn't respect it enough at Adenauer. It taught me."

02 — Team Väisänen: A Shared Effort

While Väisänen inevitably attracted the headlines, the race itself was a world away from his usual single-seater drives — instead, it was a collective effort from one of the most unusual line-ups on the grid. Alex Thompson, the Mercedes junior who had spent his GT3 Spring Challenge season oscillating between brilliance and disaster, was brought in by Väisänen as the team's endurance specialist — the driver who had been coached by the Finn for three months on exactly how to drive a GT3 car.

Thompson ran the opening stint with a calm that had been entirely absent at Sebring, Long Beach, and Goiânia. His instructions were specific: establish the car's behaviour, do not take risks, hand it over clean. He did all three. The coaching had done something — the erratic Mercedes junior who had crashed out of half his GT3 season was suddenly a metronome in the Eifel forest.

The three drivers — a championship leader, a fearless rookie, and a junior on the rise — avoided the major mistakes that often define this race after the early scare, and maintained a strong pace through changing weather and dense traffic. Whether it was Thompson steadying the opening stints, MaraDöner recovering from his error, or Väisänen closing the race with metronomic consistency, the #160 crew spent much of the race either in the top ten or climbing back toward it.

03 — Springfield's Overnight Heroics

Perhaps the most impressive individual performance came overnight, when the Nordschleife famously becomes even more intimidating under darkness and colder track conditions. It was during this period that Sarah Springfield, the Aston Martin F1 driver sharing the #817 Red Bull-liveried Vantage with Lukus Wright and Linus Lundqvist, arguably delivered her strongest contribution.

The Aston Martin was rear-heavy, prone to snap oversteer in cold conditions, and Wright — for all his dirt-track instincts and IMSA experience — had spent his night stint losing four positions as he struggled to trust the car at its limit. "I know how to drive a car," he said afterward, in the specific way that racing drivers say it when they mean the opposite. "I didn't know how to drive that car. There's a difference."

Springfield took over at hour nine in drizzle — the Eifel rain arriving exactly as the weathermen had said it wouldn't — and within three laps had found two seconds per lap that Wright had been unable to access. Her adaptability, honed across short ovals, IndyCar, and the Indianapolis 500, translated across disciplines in a way that surprised everyone except Springfield herself. In four hours she gained seven positions, reading wet patches, tyre temperatures, and the Vantage's rear behaviour with an instinctive throttle modulation that Lundqvist described afterward as "something you either have or you don't."

"I learned more in those four hours at Indianapolis than I have in any training day," Springfield said. "You learn patience. You learn that the car behind is your problem to manage, not theirs. The Nordschleife is not an oval but the principle is the same."

04 — Vettel's Return: Three Hours from the Finish, a Lifetime from Retirement

The #67 Audi RS GT3 Touring was never going to win. It was a saloon car with a roof, carrying a four-time world champion who had not raced competitively in nearly a decade, and two current F1 drivers — Robin Keisner and Lucas Koopman — who had never driven a 24-hour race in their lives. But the car, and the men inside it, became the emotional heart of the weekend.

The problem was not speed. All three had that. The problem was that none of them had the accumulated experience required to turn speed into a 24-hour GT3 result at the Nürburgring. Keisner had the racecraft but not the endurance habits. Koopman had reasonable pace but little experience managing traffic over long stints. Vettel had the smoothness and car control of a world champion but almost a decade away from competitive racing. And unlike the other F1 entries, there was no established endurance specialist in the team to organise the other two.

The result was a slow race — thirty-first overall, eleventh in the Am class, 127 laps completed — but one that ended with a standing ovation. Vettel, who was given the honour of the final three-lap stint by his co-drivers, brought the car across the line with both hands on the wheel and sat in it for forty seconds without moving. "I forgot," he said later. "I forgot what it felt like. Not the driving — the driving comes back immediately. I forgot what it felt like when the car stops and you realise you've been somewhere for 24 hours and you're still there."

The crowd on the banking above the finish straight gave the wagon a standing ovation that lasted three minutes. Several of them were crying. The Audi had not won, but it had finished. And for three drivers who had arrived with very different expectations, that was enough.

05 — A Never-Before-Seen Atmosphere at the Nordschleife

The 24h Nürburgring is already one of endurance racing's most iconic events, but the presence of seven current Formula 1 drivers — including the championship leader and a returning legend — elevated attention around the race to another level. Global media interest surged throughout the week, with the paddock buzzing from Thursday morning when the three F1-connected entries took their first laps in practice.

Even after the chequered flag, the images lingered. Väisänen standing by the #160 Porsche, still in his race suit, debriefing with Thompson and MaraDöner as the Eifel sun set behind them. Springfield, arms crossed on the pitwall, watching Lundqvist bring the Aston Martin home in fourteenth. And Vettel, forty seconds of stillness in the cockpit of the Audi, a four-time world champion who had remembered what it felt like to finish something this hard.

The Nürburgring 2026 was not about who won. It was about what the old circuit gave to those who came. The Nordschleife does not care who you are. But sometimes, if you respect it enough, it lets you leave with something you did not have when you arrived.
